data.content_ref: inline:{"claim": "Two conclusions are the same claim iff they occupy identical causal roles in the system's decision-making, meaning they have the same downstream effects on all actions and further inferences under all possible inputs.", "mechanism": "The system constructs a causal graph of its belief dependencies and action policies. When two independently derived conclusions are detected to agree, the system intervenes on each (e.g., by temporarily suppresing one) and observes whether any decision or inference changes. If the causal impact on every output node is identical, they are merged into a single node.", "scope": {"covers": ["deterministic reasoning systems with a fixed action repertoire", "conclusions that influence decisions or further inferences"], "excludes": ["purely epistemic claims with no downstream effects", "systems without a clear causal model of their own reasoning"]}, "forbidden": [{"case": "Two conclusions have identical causal impact in all tested scenarios but one is a logical tautology and the other is a contingent fact that happens to hold in all tested scenarios; merging them later causes a contradiction when a new scenario makes the contingent fact false while the tautology remains true.", "eval": "program:causal_equivalence_contradiction_check"}], "prose_notes": "This criterion risks over-merging when the system's causal model is incomplete, mistaking accidental co-extension for identity. It risks under-merging when the causal model is too fine-grained, treating logically equivalent statements as distinct because they have different internal representations."}
